issue.issue_text: whether the finding of guilt of the appellants arrived at by the High Court is sustainable in light of the evidence on record.

law.law_text: In a case based on circumstantial evidence, the chain of evidence must be complete and lead to an inescapable conclusion of guilt.
The prosecution has the burden to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt.

To reverse a finding of acquittal, a higher threshold is required. The appellate court must find the trial court's view to be completely unsustainable, perverse, or illegal, not merely that an alternate view is possible. This is because the presumption of innocence is strengthened by an acquittal.

application.fact_application: The Court analyzed the evidence and found that the prosecution failed to discharge its burden of proof. The case, being based on circumstantial evidence, was far from meeting the standard of a complete chain of evidence leading to an inescapable conclusion of guilt.

The Court identified 'irreconcilable' reasonable doubts that struck at the foundation of the prosecution's case. It noted that the link of causation between the accused persons and the alleged murder was 'conspicuously missing'.

The Court also found that the High Court's approach in reversing the acquittal of two of the accused (A-6 and A-7) was not in line with settled law. The High Court took a 'cursory view' and reversed the acquittal without finding any illegality, perversity, or impossibility in the Trial Court's reasoning.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the finding of guilt by the High Court was not sustainable. It held that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt, as the circumstantial evidence was insufficient. Furthermore, the High Court had erred by not adhering to the high legal threshold required to reverse an acquittal. Consequently, the Court set aside the convictions and acquitted all the appellants.

issue.issue_text: whether the approach of the High Court was in line with the settled law for reversing an acquittal into conviction in a criminal appeal.

facts: The High Court reversed the Trial Court's decision to acquit two accused persons (A-6 and A-7).
The Trial Court had acquitted them after a thorough appreciation of the evidence.
The High Court's reason for reversal was that the acquittal was based on the statement of a witness (PW5) which it found improbable and decided to exclude from the record.
law: To reverse a finding of acquittal, a higher threshold is required because the presumption of innocence in favor of an accused is strengthened by an acquittal.
An acquittal cannot be reversed merely because an alternative view of the evidence is possible.
The appellate court must find that the Trial Court's view was completely unsustainable, illegal, perverse, impossible, or that the Trial Court failed to appreciate the evidence.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court took a "cursory view" of the matter.
The High Court failed to meet the required legal standard because it did not arrive at any finding of illegality, perversity, or impossibility in the Trial Court's view.
The High Court also did not make a positive finding of the involvement of the two accused persons.
By simply excluding one witness's testimony as the basis for reversal, the High Court did not properly apply the settled law for overturning an acquittal.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court's approach was not in line with the settled law and that it erred in reversing the acquittal of the two accused persons.

cases.principle: To summarize the settled law regarding the approach of the High Court for reversing an acquittal into a conviction.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The approach of an appellate court must be in line with the settled law for reversing an acquittal into a conviction in a criminal appeal.
obiter: A sweeping observation by a court is legally untenable and highly objectionable when it is not commensurate with judicial sensitivity and neutrality, and is not based on any evidence on record.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The prosecution failed to discharge its burden to prove the case beyond a reasonable doubt, as the reasonable doubts were irreconcilable and struck at the foundation of its case. The conviction could not be sustained because it relied on the improbable and unreliable testimony of interested family members whose presence at the scene was doubtful, while the prosecution failed to examine readily available independent public witnesses, and the alleged motive was insufficient on its own.
legal_tests_applied: The prosecution has the burden to prove the case beyond a reasonable doubt.
If two views are possible from the evidence on record, an appellate court must be extremely slow in interfering with an appeal against acquittal.

When the version put forth by interested witnesses comes under a shadow of doubt, the rule of prudence demands that independent public witnesses must be examined and corroborating material must be gathered, especially when such witnesses are readily available.

Motive has a bearing only when the evidence on record is sufficient to prove the ingredients of the offences; the case cannot succeed on the presence of motive alone without the proof of foundational facts.
why_appellant_lost: The prosecution's case was rendered improbable and unreliable due to the non-examination of natural, independent public witnesses who were admittedly present at the scene of the crime.
The prosecution's case relied on eyewitnesses who were family members, and their natural presence at the place of occurrence was under serious doubt.

The alleged motive was a 'double-edged sword' as it could have operated both ways in a family property dispute, and motive alone is insufficient to sustain a conviction without foundational proof of the crime.
The cumulative effect of the doubts in the prosecution's case was irreconcilable and struck at the foundation of its case, leading to a failure to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.
policy_considerations: A sweeping observation by a court that is not based on any evidence on record is not only legally untenable but also highly objectionable, as it is not commensurate with the sensitivity and neutrality expected from a court of law.
